title: Localization accuracy in single-molecule fluorescence microscopy
authors: Chapman, K. B.; Schmidt, R.; Engelhardt, J.; Hell, S. W.
abstract: The two prevalent methods to determine the position of individual fluorophores in the focal plane of a microscope rely either on the centroid of the fluorescence pattern produced by the fluorophore on a camera or on targeting the fluorophore's coordinate with a spatially controlled illumination minimum, as realized in MINFLUX. In both methods, (sub)nanometer localization precisions have been reached, but little is known about their accuracy, i.e., the deviation of the obtained coordinate from its ground truth. Here we report a theoretical and experimental comparison of the accuracy provided by these two strategies. We quantify substantial systematic errors in camera-based localization due to the interplay of two difficult-to-control parameters: the orientation of the fluorophore in space and its axial deviation from the focal plane (defocus). For example, within an axial range of {+/-}120 nm around the focus, the median distance between two fluorophores on a nanobody measured by camera-based localization varies by 26.5 nm. Under the same conditions, a commercial MINFLUX system yields a median variation in distance of 1.4 nm, indicating an improvement in accuracy by an order of magnitude. The accuracy of MINFLUX localization can be further improved to (sub-)[a]ngstrom levels by reducing the average distance between the coordinates targeted by the illumination minimum and the fluorophore. As it delivers unrivaled precision and accuracy for mapping fluorophores and their distances, we consider coordinate-targeted localization essential for studying labeled cells at the sub-10 nm level and for exploring structural and conformational changes of labeled biomolecules.

title: Childhood Trauma and Cortical Thickness in Bipolar Disorder with and without Psychosis: Effects by Diagnostic Group and Trauma Subtype
authors: Chapagai, D.; Hodges, G.; Mutraji, A.; Turner, J. A.
abstract: Abstract Background Bipolar disorder affects about 2-3% of the population and is associated with cortical abnormalities, with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP) reported to show more pronounced changes. It remains unclear whether childhood trauma is associated with cortical thickness differences across bipolar disorder subgroups, particularly in BDP. Methods Using the publicly available PARDIP (Psychosis and Affective Research Domains and Intermediate Phenotypes) data set, we examined whether childhood trauma was associated with cortical thickness differences among 120 individuals: 33 with bipolar disorder without psychosis (BD; 36% male), 38 with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP; 47% male), and 49 healthy controls (HC; 61% male). Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form (CTQ-SF), and T1-weighted MRI scans were processed with FreeSurfer to extract cortical thickness across the 68 Desikan-Killiany regions. Linear mixed effects models tested associations between CTQ subtype scores and cortical thickness and trauma-by-diagnosis interactions, with sensitivity analyses for medication class and illness duration following the ENIGMA guidelines. Results No cortical thickness difference survived correction for multiple testing. At the nominal level, BD showed reduced thickness relative to HC in cingulate, frontal and occipital regions, whereas BDP showed greater superior temporal thickness relative to BD. Sexual abuse was nominally associated with reduced temporal thickness. Exploratory trauma-by-diagnosis interactions suggested region- and subtype-specific patterns that did not survive correction. Medication class and illness duration showed no significant effects after FDR correction. Conclusions These exploratory findings suggest nominal, region-specific associations between childhood trauma subtypes and cortical thickness in bipolar disorder. However, no findings survived correction for multiple comparisons, so they should be read as preliminary and need replication in larger samples.

title: A Chronnectogram-ICA Framework for Tracking Continuously Evolving and Overlapping Functional Brain States
authors: Soleimani, N.; Wiafe, S.-L.; Iraji, A.; Preda, A.; Pearlson, G.; Adali, T.; Calhoun, V.
abstract: The discrete-state model of brain dynamics has become the dominant paradigm in functional connectivity analysis, representing network activity as transitions among a fixed set of transiently recurring states while generally assuming that the states themselves do not evolve. We introduce a multilevel chronnectogram framework that relaxes this assumption and explicitly represents the higher-order temporal structure of brain dynamics, how distinct states couple and co-evolve over time, alongside the persistence of each state. The method integrates spatially guided independent component analysis (ICA) with subject-specific, state-guided dynamic ICA to capture evolving and overlapping connectivity patterns in a shared representational space. Validation on simulations with known ground truth shows recovery of continuous overlap and higher-order coupling structure invisible to discrete-state methods. Applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging from the FBIRN dataset (151 schizophrenia, 160 controls), the framework reveals that the same pair of brain states is shifted toward opposite extremes across patients, with strong synchrony in some and active anti-coupling in others, creating a redistribution of connectivity regimes invisible to conventional occupancy metrics, providing a substrate in which schizophrenia can appear both hyper- and hypo-volatile depending on the measure applied.

title: Breadboard Neuroscience: Exploring Neuronal Dynamics and Computation with Simple Electronic Circuits
abstract: Simple electronic circuits provide a tangible means of exploring the electrical principles underlying neuronal signalling and computation. Here is presented a sequence of experiments using inexpensive, readily available components assembled on solderless breadboards to investigate passive membrane properties and analogue neural computation. A resistor-capacitor membrane model demonstrates how membrane resistance, capacitance, and excitatory conductance determine response amplitude and charging and discharging time constants. Multiple inputs illustrate sublinear summation and shunting inhibition. Connecting membrane compartments through axial resistances reproduces spatial attenuation and temporal delay. We then construct an elementary motion detector to demonstrate how simple electrical operations can produce direction-selective responses to visual motion. Together, this approach offers an accessible and flexible platform for exploring neuronal biophysics, allowing students to relate mathematical descriptions to observable electrical behaviour whilst developing practical electronics skills and engaging creatively in the design of their own experiments.

title: Systematic comparison of color representations between humans and deep neural networks: towards predicting human color perception in a vast color space
abstract: The representational structure of human color perception across a vast color space remains incompletely understood. While classical studies measured numerous color pairs, these measurements compared only similar colors, and exploring the global relationships among thousands of colors has been infeasible due to the time costs of psychophysical experiments. Given these constraints, deep neural networks (DNNs) have attracted attention as a promising tool for providing proxies or predictions of human perception beyond psychophysical experiments. However, it remains unclear which DNNs possess embeddings that geometrically align with human color perception. Furthermore, it is unclear which learning paradigm enables DNNs to acquire a color representation that aligns with that of humans. Here, we systematically investigate which learning paradigm enables DNNs to produce a color representation that is structurally congruent with that of humans, with a focus on three types: self-supervised learning (SSL) that trains on images alone by image reconstruction, supervised learning (SL) that trains on images with category labels, and contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) that trains on image-text pairs. We compared the embeddings of DNNs with the human similarity judgments of 93 colors using a rigorous unsupervised method, Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport (GWOT). Our results show that, while each learning paradigm acquires color representations that strongly align with human data at the fine-item level in early layers, only CLIP sustains such a representation at the output. Furthermore, when we leveraged a key advantage of DNNs and investigated the representational structure of 4096 colors, the early layers of each learning paradigm and the output of CLIP consistently converged on their own characteristic structures. These structures present plausible predictions for the large-scale human color representation. Our work demonstrates an approach for exploring unknown territories of human perception using computational models validated in a limited empirical space, and provides predictions for future large-scale psychophysical experiments.

title: Neocortical Feedback Biases Hippocampal Reactivation Toward Unconsolidated Memories in a Predictive-Coding Model of Systems Consolidation
abstract: During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: some memory traces, such as newly acquired or weakly learned ones, are preferentially reactivated. These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memory traces, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems. The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop hippocampal-neocortical dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dialogue itself rather than from an explicit scheduler. In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memory patterns. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated patterns, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new patterns were incrementally added during transfer. Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient transfer of memory content during systems consolidation.

title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory
authors: Kerren, C.; Dixit, S.; Coxon, E.; Nikolaev, A. R.; Doeller, C. F.
abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but contributes to the construction and organisation of episodic representations. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixations are integrated into an evolving internal representation, subsequently stored in associative memory and later retrieved through partial reinstatement of the original sampling trajectory. Within to-be-remembered elements, successive samples support progressive individuation; between elements, more frequent transitions strengthen relational binding. As sampling proceeds, internal representations become progressively lower-dimensional while retaining information about where samples were taken and when they occurred in the sequence. Sampling history also remains embedded in the resulting representation: changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the representation itself and element-specific retrieval. At retrieval, reinstating more of the original sampling trajectory improves access to specific elements, while competition is strongest when memories share both semantic category and sampling history. Finally, an exploratory generative readout shows that regions sampled during encoding are reconstructed more faithfully than unsampled regions. Together, these findings suggest that sequential sampling provides a candidate computational process through which episodic representations are constructed, shaping their subsequent storage and retrieval.

title: A reinforcement learning framework for goal-directed stimulation of engineered neuronal networks
authors: Maurer, B.; Vasiliauskaite, V.; Hengsteler, J.; Cathomen, G.; Ruff, T.; Schmid, C.; Vörös, J.; Ihle, S. J.
abstract: Systematically perturbing neuronal circuits under controlled conditions offers a promising route to understanding how they encode and process information, yet remains methodologically demanding. In vitro neuronal networks can be cultured on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) that allow stimulation and recording, and microfluidic patterning can constrain network topology to yield stable stimulation-evoked responses. Yet, the space of possible spatiotemporal stimulation patterns remains too large for exhaustive exploration. Additionally, the evoked responses depend on prior stimulation history. Here, we present an open-source framework that sustains closed-loop reinforcement-learning (RL) control of engineered neuronal networks, sending electrical stimuli to the MEA and evaluating the evoked responses to identify stimulation patterns that drive specific target activity motifs. We extend inkube, a low-cost, open-source electrophysiology system from off-the-shelf components, with closed-loop electrophysiology. This enables reliable delivery of stimulation at single-sample precision with millisecond-range round-trip times. It also allows independent RL agents to control multiple networks simultaneously. As a proof-of-principle application, we benchmarked different agents on the task of identifying stimulation patterns that maximise the length of clockwise-circular firing sequences. We first demonstrated that stimulation-evoked responses in engineered recurrent networks were stable and separable across the action space over hours of continuous operation. We characterised the dependency of responses on prior stimulation history, finding state dependence in a subset of stimulus pairs. The agents learned to improve reward during training with respect to random stimulation. Agents converged on non-trivial stimulation patterns that span the full action space rather than mirroring the target motif. All hardware designs and software are publicly available, providing an accessible platform for goal-directed functional characterisation of engineered neuronal networks at single-spike resolution.

title: Analysis of gene expression changes after Latrunculin B-induced actin depolymerization
authors: Kargas, G.; Layden, M. J.; Vavylonis, D.
abstract: Links between the cytoskeleton and gene expression are increasingly appreciated. The cytoskeleton dynamically regulates its own expression and organization through transcriptional feedback loops that sense cellular concentrations and mechanical forces. Disruption of cytoskeletal dynamics can also influence cell fate. However, the breadth, temporal dynamics, and mechanistic basis of the cytoskeleton-transcription coupling have yet to be fully resolved. To characterize this response more broadly, we re-analyzed time-resolved bulk RNA-seq data that were previously used to demonstrate that treatment with actin depolymerization drug Latrunculin B (LatB) drives differentiation of human pancreatic progenitor cells in culture. Beyond the previously identified induction of cell differentiation, we find that LatB produced extensive transcriptional changes within the actin cytoskeleton, including downregulation of actin, myosin II heavy chains, myosin I, tropomyosins, -actinins, filamins, talin, vinculin and plastin. The changes were not restricted to the actin system, but extended to microtubule and intermediate filament systems, with noticeable changes in the expression of KIF19, MAP1A, MAP1B, Type I and II keratins and Type IV neurofilaments. More broadly, the response extended to genes involved in transcription, vesicle trafficking, metabolism, translation, ion transport, protein homeostasis, and cell signaling. The breadth of this response suggested engagement of multiple transcriptional regulatory programs. Transcription factor activity inference using decoupleR identified MRTF/SRF as the most inactivated TF network, consistent with its known role in actin homeostasis, in addition to Hippo/YAP-TEAD, MYC, stress-response and other pathways. These results provide the broader landscape of cellular response to actin depolymerization, serving as a foundation for future studies to distinguish general mechanisms of cytoskeletal homeostasis from differentiation-associated responses, and to narrow the underlying regulatory mechanisms linking cytoskeletal state to gene expression.

title: Lef1 Promotes Foxi1-Dependent Ionocyte Specification by Airway Submucosal Gland Progenitors
authors: Shahin, W.; Hajibabazade, J.; Snyder, O.; Fritz, G.; Yuan, F.; Ievlev, V.; Lynch, T.; Yeaman, C. A.; Engelhardt, J. F.
abstract: Pulmonary ionocytes are rare cells in submucosal gland (SMG)-containing airways thought to have specialized ion transport properties that regulate airway surface fluid and mucus composition. The origins of pulmonary ionocytes remain unclear, but their association with airway SMGs suggests they may arise from specialized progenitors in this compartment. We show that mouse glandular myoepithelial cells (GMECs) have a unique capacity to specify ionocytes enriched in the Cftr channel. The Lef1 transcription factor was both necessary and sufficient to promote GMEC specification of ionocytes in mouse trachea, 3D organoids, and/or air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures. Overexpression of Lef1 (Lef1OE) in GMECs produced ionocyte-enriched epithelia with enhanced Cftr-mediated chloride, bicarbonate, and fluid transport properties. Moreover, Foxi1 knockout in Lef1OE GMECs prevented ionocyte formation while promoting specification of Cftr-expressing secretory cells. These findings provide a progenitor relationship for the anatomical association of ionocytes with SMGs and a transcriptional framework for coordinated specification of CFTR-expressing ionocytes and secretory cells.

title: Sequence sensitivity of open chromatin reveals constrained regulatory elements underlying human traits
authors: Tomizuka, K.; Koido, M.; Suzuki, A.; Yoshino, S.; Tanaka, N.; Ishikawa, Y.; Liu, X.; Koyama, S.; Ishigaki, K.; Murakawa, Y.; Immune transcript/enhancer consortium (ITEC),  ; Yamamoto, K.; Terao, C.
abstract: Open chromatin regions (OCRs) delineate cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes across the genome, yet their functional importance varies considerably. Here, we introduce CAMBUS (Chromatin Accessibility Mutation Burden Score), a machine-learning framework that quantifies the sensitivity of predicted chromatin accessibility to sequence perturbation to prioritize functionally important OCRs. Applying CAMBUS to 29 immune cell types, we identified 66,043 CAMBUS-defined OCRs (cOCRs), without directly incorporating human genetic variation or existing evolutionary constraint metrics. Nevertheless, cOCRs were strongly enriched in independently defined constrained regions (odds ratio (OR)=11.45 (95% confidence interval (CI) 9.33-14.05), P=4.7 x 10-68), and active regulatory elements, with enrichment for super-enhancers remaining after adjustment for established constraint metrics and sequence features (OR=6.18 (95% CI 3.80-10.05), P=2.1 x 10-13). cOCRs also showed cell-type-specific enrichment for the heritability of immune-mediated diseases and for putative causal variants identified by statistical fine-mapping across European and East Asian ancestries, including rare variants. Integration with statistical fine-mapping further linked 1,533 putative causal variants across 70 complex traits to cell-type-specific cOCRs, revealing plausible regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits. Together, CAMBUS provides a region-centered framework for identifying regulatory elements whose predicted activity is sensitive to sequence disruption and that are enriched for evolutionary constraint, complementing existing regulatory and constraint annotations for interpreting non-coding genetic variation.

title: Engineering potent avian GPR25 agonists using an ostrich CXCL17 gene relic
authors: Yu, J.; Li, H.-Z.; Wang, J.-J.; Liu, Y.-L.; Guo, Z.-Y.
abstract: C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CXCL17) activates G protein-coupled receptor 25 (GPR25) in most vertebrate lineages. Although birds appear to have lost functional CXCL17, CXCL17 gene relics and intact GPR25 genes persist in certain taxa. This study investigated whether a fragment encoded by an avian CXCL17 gene relic could guide the engineering of potent agonists for avian GPR25s. A 22-residue C-terminal fragment encoded by African ostrich CXCL17 gene relic was grafted onto the corresponding position of loggerhead turtle or human CXCL17, and the resulting hybrids were prepared via bacterial overexpression and functionally characterized via cell-based assays. The turtle-ostrich and human-ostrich CXCL17 hybrids showed no detectable activity at turtle or human GPR25 but exhibited substantially greater potency than their parental proteins at two avian GPR25s in {beta}-arrestin recruitment assays, with half-maximal effective concentrations of approximately 25 and 100 nM at the ostrich receptor and 5 and 13 nM at the mallard receptor, respectively. Both hybrids bound directly to the ostrich or mallard GPR25 in homogenous ligand-receptor binding assays and induced migration of transfected cells expressing the ostrich or mallard receptor in chemotaxis assays. These findings demonstrate that a fragment encoded by the ostrich CXCL17 gene relic confers potent avian GPR25 agonism and establishes the C-terminus as the primary driver of species selectivity. These hybrids provide functional surrogate tools for probing avian GPR25 biology.

title: Myopathy-causing variants of PYROXD1 converge on impaired RNA ligation
authors: Guzman-Perez, S.; Kleinwaechter, M.; Ozeren, M. S.; Catharin, A.; Weitzer, S.; Milasinovic, M.; Yaman, M. B.; Gorbenkova, A.; Hahn, M.; Koglgruber, R.; Hollenstein, D.; Penninger, J. M.; Hartl, M.; Cooper, S. T.; Evesson, F. J.; Martinez, J.; Asanovic, I.
abstract: RNA ligation is critical for RNA processing pathways including pre-tRNA splicing. RTCB is the only essential RNA ligase in humans and the catalytic subunit of the tRNA ligase complex (tRNA-LC). Its active site is sensitive to oxidation and strictly depends on oxidoreductase PYROXD1, the only tRNA-LC subunit with multiple known pathogenic protein-coding variants. The role of RNA ligation in PYROXD1 myopathy remained contentious: loss of PYROXD1 primarily affects mitochondria, and ligation-linked readouts are inconsistent in existing assays. Here, we reveal that PYROXD1 is physically, genetically and functionally committed to the tRNA-LC. Selectively impairing RTCB activation reproduces hallmarks of PYROXD1 dysfunction, including mitochondrial deregulation. Using degron-based depletion of endogenous PYROXD1, we show that all six single amino acid variants reported in patients fail to sustain RNA ligation in proportion to their clinical severity. The variants segregate into three mechanistic classes: they lower protein stability, disrupt the NADPH-mediated conformational switch, or impair RTCB engagement by the C-terminal tail, a sequence unique to PYROXD1 and directly affected in the most severe variant D500N. Variant-level measurements in the degron model predict outcomes in homozygous and compound heterozygous patient fibroblasts. Together, these data establish impaired RNA ligation as the driver of PYROXD1 pathogenicity.

title: A Unified Framework for Batch Correction and Imputation in Modern Mass Spectrometry Proteomics
authors: Anwar, A. M.; Bayoumi, S.; Lahti, L.; Coffey, E.
abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics, including single-cell applications, are often confounded by batch effects, inter-laboratory variation, and signal drift that can obscure biological interpretation. NMFBatch addresses these sources of unwanted variation through a unified framework that combines non-negative matrix factorization with generalized additive modelling to jointly capture discrete and continuous technical effects from protein expression data. It handles missing values directly through masking and on-the-fly imputation. Benchmarking across reference datasets, plasma proteomics cohorts, simulations, and single-cell data demonstrated that NMFBatch reduced technical variation while preserving biological structure. These results establish NMFBatch as a robust framework for batch correction, harmonization, and integrative proteomics analysis from protein expression data.

title: From coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to continuum models of biomolecular condensation
authors: Hubman, A.; Potisk, T.; Merzel, F.
abstract: Biomolecular condensation contributes to cellular organization and the regulation of numerous biochemical processes. Capturing its dynamics on large spatio-temporal scales requires a macroscopic model that accurately describes both thermodynamic forces and molecular transport. Here, we investigate the applicability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation for modeling phase-separation dynamics in intrinsically disordered proteins. Using the low-complexity domain of FUS as a model system for biomolecular condensation, we perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to infer the free-energy functional and mobility coefficient entering the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The resulting continuum model accurately describes the growth of initial concentration fluctuations in the spinodal regime and the subsequent morphological evolution of the concentration fields during coarsening. We find that the free-energy functional is transferable across different stages of phase separation, whereas the mobility is not. During coarsening, we identify two kinetic regimes characterized by distinct mobilities, which persist even when a concentration-dependent mobility is introduced.
